method: Each registered concrete format was traced from its YAML definition through its emitter and compared with an official specification or public primary exemplar. Optional fields were assessed as a source-fidelity surface, not as a requirement to emit every possible field.

formats.notes: Epoch comment lines followed by commands match Bash history-file timestamp semantics.

The supported 302/305/106/733 families and classic ASA prefix are source-shaped. The format models a bounded message subset and classic timestamp mode rather than every current ASA logging option. Post-review remediation moved static/dynamic NAT address views and PAT lifetime into each frozen sensor observation so build/teardown and inbound ICMP projections share the owning connection's facts.

The object/action/properties model and UUID relationships follow the public OpTC eCAR description. EvidenceForge extends the public object/action vocabulary, while no versioned machine-readable upstream schema exists; interoperability therefore cannot be claimed beyond this documented dialect. The corrected public dataset also documents identifier/property defects in the original corpus.
The prefix is combined-log shaped, but absolute URLs/CONNECT targets and the trailing quoted metadata block are an EvidenceForge proxy dialect, not an Apache or Nginx standard combined format.

Timestamp, generator/signature/revision tuple, classification, priority, protocol, and endpoints match the fast-alert family. Snort 3 exemplars quote messages and may include AppID; the generated line is closer to a common Snort 2/Suricata-compatible variant. Post-review remediation evaluates validated structured signature predicates against the finalized transport and protocol transaction before this source-local projection is admitted.

The PRI/version/timestamp/hostname/app/procid/msgid/structured-data layout follows RFC 5424. Format validation does not enforce the RFC token-length and character constraints for APP-NAME, PROCID, MSGID, and HOSTNAME.
The record morphology matches the NCSA combined log format.

The XML event envelope and supported Security payloads are source-shaped for the reviewed event subset. Event 4648 now uses the provider-manifest IpAddress/IpPort names; Network Address and Port are display labels, not XML field names. Microsoft defines EventRecordID as the record number assigned when an event is logged and documents sequential numbering; post-review remediation models omitted selected-channel rows from elapsed time instead of independent gaps. The emitter is a selected-event renderer, not an EVTX writer, and fixed provider/task/version metadata creates a maintenance obligation as Windows variants evolve.

Supported event shapes and UTC timestamps align with Sysmon. Sysmon EventRecordIDs share the Windows channel-sequence contract and post-review elapsed-time gap model but use an independent per-host Sysmon channel epoch. Shared destination hostname and one ProcessGuid path are recomputed in the emitter, violating cross-source ownership even when individual rows remain source-shaped.

JSON fields, originator/responder semantics, UID, state, history, and accounting match Zeek's connection model. Zeek documents service as the set of confirmed services and raises analyzer-confirmation events when a protocol is confirmed; post-review remediation therefore clears non-ICMP service labels on payload-free connections.

Field morphology is Zeek-compatible. Minimal environments can render the same address as client, server, and assignment, which is an upstream world-planning defect rather than an emitter-format defect.
Tuple, transaction, query, response-code, flag, answer, TTL, rejection, and opcode fields match Zeek JSON conventions.

FUID, host lists, connection joins, analyzer, byte accounting, timeout, and hash fields match the files framework. The baseline review found file observations ending 1-2 ms after their parent conn interval. Post-review Batch 3 remediation makes protocol/file projections consume the frozen sensor transaction interval; the final integrated probe reports zero file or protocol-child interval escapes.
Connection tuple, transaction depth, request/response morphology, file joins, and MIME arrays match Zeek's HTTP log.
NTP fields are source-shaped and dynamic probes require a response-bearing parent connection.

Field names and FUID semantics follow Zeek. EvidenceForge requires nextUpdate in its local schema, narrowing upstream optionality and producing a recognizable completeness fingerprint. All 36 integrated OCSP-response file observations have an exact 0.02-second duration, adding a source-visible synthetic fingerprint.
Node/filter/init/success morphology matches Zeek's packet-filter diagnostic examples.
FUID, compile time, architecture, subsystem, mitigation, table, and section fields follow Zeek PE analysis.
Timestamp, level, message, and location match Zeek reporter diagnostics.
Connection, SMTP envelope/header, path, TLS, depth, and file-join fields follow Zeek SMTP.

Tuple, UID, TLS version/cipher/SNI, resumption, establishment, history, and certificate joins are compatible. Uniform omission of other common optional fields such as curve and next_protocol is a potential synthetic fingerprint.
The record shape is compatible, but no production SecurityEvent constructor attaches WeirdContext; the registered format is reachable only through direct emitter tests/raw behavior.
FUID, fingerprint, certificate namespace, SAN, CA constraint, and client/host flags match Zeek X.509 JSON conventions.

limitations: The SOF-ELK® and Splunk container-backed parser tests could not run because no Docker/Podman Compose daemon was available; Splunk additionally requires explicit license acceptance.
No proprietary production corpus was used. Review relied on public official documentation and public-domain or public research exemplars.
eCAR has a public prose description and corpus but no stable versioned machine-readable upstream schema; EvidenceForge interoperability is therefore assessed as a dialect, not certified conformance.
